common_name: Nainital Windmill Palm (Extra-Hardy Himalayan Seed Strain)

planting.note: Set out container-grown palms once the soil has warmed after the last frost, in full sun to light shade with well-drained, fertile soil. Give roots a full growing season to settle in before the first real test of winter cold.

directions: This seed strain traces to wild windmill palm populations found near Nainital in the Kumaon foothills of the Indian Himalaya, a high-elevation zone shared with the even hardier Trachycarpus takil, and some growers suspect the strain carries genes from natural crossing between the two. Foliage is noticeably stiffer and more rigid than typical nursery-grown Trachycarpus fortunei, and established specimens have reportedly shrugged off brief drops to 0 degrees F, making this one of the most cold-tolerant trunking palm strains a Gulf Coast gardener can plant as insurance against rare arctic outbreaks. Growth is slower than generic windmill palm, especially while the trunk is still forming, so choose a permanent site and be patient. Water deeply through the first two summers to build a strong root system, then reduce irrigation to occasional deep soaks during dry spells.

common_name: Taylor's Hardy Windmill Palm (Raleigh Cold-Hardy Seed Strain)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown palms after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a site with some wind shelter so the large fronds are not shredded in storms.

directions: This strain descends from a single windmill palm planted decades ago at a Raleigh, North Carolina nursery that came through a record-setting subzero winter undamaged while a sibling tree beside it did not, and offspring grown from its seed are now planted throughout the Raleigh area, including in local park palm collections. It is slow to size up in its first few years but accelerates noticeably in trunk and frond growth once established, eventually forming a full, bold-textured crown typical of the species. Because the tested cold tolerance comes from a piedmont North Carolina winter rather than a humid Gulf climate, give it fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil rather than the leaner, drier conditions some other hardy strains tolerate. Remove spent fronds as they brown and provide a somewhat sheltered exposure to keep the large leaves from tearing in strong coastal wind.
